title: Software is not neutral
introduction: This week we learned that software is not neutral. It helps us, but it also tells us how to work. We did a class exercise called "Break Microsoft" to feel this. We also had our first HyperText Markup Language (HTML) and Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) workshops, so this week I started to read and change real code.
related_work:
Three works inspired me. The Sheep Market by Aaron Koblin (Image 1) [1]: he asks lots of people to each make a small part, and together they finish one big project. It makes me think about the factory workers who make e-cigarettes for very low pay. Anatomy of an AI System (Image 2) [2] shows a smart speaker from birth to death. They study the smart speaker, and I study the e-cigarette: I want to find the hidden cost behind every part. A Single Div by Lynn Fisher (Image 3) [3] uses only Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) to make her drawings. I will also use CSS to make my pictures move and to change the colour of the words.

Reading 1 is about the advantages and disadvantages of social media for artists. The algorithm makes it easy to find ideas, but it can also close you in a filter bubble. I agree that a small community, like our class, helps more than a big platform [4]. In Reading 2, one picture shows a machine that turns music into a painting, but it also makes smoke. My project has the same meaning: the battery and other parts of e-cigarettes may harm the environment [5].
method:
In Break Microsoft, the task was to make something on paper that Word cannot make. I tore the paper and put water stains on it. I coloured my finger with a marker pen and pressed it on the paper like a stamp. I also wrote words one by one in a circle, and I drew a small picture. Then we swapped our work and tried to copy each other's in Word (Images 5 and 6).

On Wednesday we had the first HTML and CSS workshop. In the evening I practised on the About Me page from the workshop: I changed the colours, the borders and the layout, and I added a colour line that was missing (Images 7 and 8).

On Friday we built a website with several pages and one navigation bar. In class I made three project cards in three colours with class and id (identifier) (Image 9). For homework I added a new page called My Page and linked it from every page (Image 10). I also drew a bigger pixel-art circuit board for my Project 0 e-cigarette (Image 11), because the first one was only a red block.
results_discussion:
I was surprised. Word has a brush tool that I had never noticed before. Most of the effects can be made in Word, just like you can also type text in Photoshop. Only the physical damage, like the torn paper, cannot be copied.

From the practice I learned that the div tag (division) is a box: you put information inside so it stays separate from the title. The ul tag (unordered list) is a box too, and inside it each li tag (list item) is one item and the a tag (anchor) is the link; they are a fixed combination. A class name is free. I can call it any name I like, as long as the HTML and the CSS use the same name. Body controls the whole page: the font, the width and the background. After this week I have some understanding of HTML and CSS.

For the blog question I chose One Million Checkboxes (Image 4) [6]. It works both ways. When 1,000 strangers click at the same time, the box I just checked is unchecked a second later. People start fighting over boxes, checking and unchecking again and again. If someone writes an automatic program (a bot) to attack, other people cannot play normally. But when strangers cooperate, they can make all kinds of pictures and messages. The author only built the platform; the people who really finished the work were the teenagers and the other players.

From Friday I learned that the ul tag holds the list, each li tag is one item, and an li only becomes a link when it has an a tag (anchor) inside. The page I am on has no link and gets the "selected" id, so it shows an underline. My Page only has two short paragraphs for now; I will fill it this weekend.
conclusion_future_work:
We also learned eight verbs of the web. My Project 0 will use most of them, except "listen" and "watch". One Million Checkboxes gave me an idea for my e-cigarette project: every time a visitor clicks the mouthpiece, it counts as one puff. After many puffs the battery is used up, and the used batteries pile up. In the end the page shows how much damage all the visitors together have done to the environment. Next week we start animation and JavaScript, so this weekend I need to practise HTML and CSS more.

At the weekend I moved my homework text from Word to my website. I found that the text was all squeezed together and the links could not be clicked. I asked AI how to solve this. To keep the line breaks, I added three lines of CSS (Image 12). For the links, AI gave me a short piece of JavaScript; I studied what each line does and typed it out by hand (Image 13). I also practised on My Page: I wrote a heading, a paragraph, a list and a link, and I changed the colour and the border with CSS (Image 14). My moodboard and my desk research (nine sources) for Project 0 are not in this post; they are on the Projects page of this site.
